text:
neeraj: Observed a subtle UX foot-gun in the Go generator sample: cancelling the caller ctx during the generator handshake sometimes leaves the consumer goroutine stuck on gen.Events(). This is affecting a few onboarding examples.

neeraj: Short repro: spawn generator, start event consumer, cancel context during handshake window. Consumer goroutine may never terminate and the sample app process lingers.

olivia: Do we have an actual goroutine leak or just blocked on I/O? If the read loop waits on the http/2 stream and the transport isn't interrupted the goroutine will naturally block. But still a poor DX.

neeraj: From stack traces in a test run I see stacks with net/http.(*http2clientConn).readFrame and our decoder.ReadEvent. That suggests the stream isn't being closed when ctx is cancelled in some middleware cases.

tarun: My suspicion: the auth middleware wraps RoundTripper but creates its own background refresh goroutine using context.Background() instead of inheriting the request ctx. If that refresh loop holds references to the transport or response body, cancel won't close the stream.

olivia: Another angle: the generator object creates an internal ctx via context.WithCancel and returns a public-facing ctx to the caller. If we ever replace or duplicate contexts poorly we can end up with an internal ctx that isn't cancelled by the caller. We should avoid creating separate, long-lived internal contexts unless strictly necessary.

neeraj: Agreed. Proposed fixes discussed: (A) ensure every http request uses req = req.WithContext(parentCtx) immediately before RoundTrip; (B) stop spawning detached goroutines for retries/refresh and instead use errgroup.WithContext or run inline; (C) add explicit Generator.Close() that cancels internal ctx and closes Events channel.

tarun: For parity with other languages, explicit Close() is a good ergonomic win (Python/JS labs often have .close() on stream-like objects). But caller confusion: should Close be required? Document it clearly: either call Close() or cancel the ctx.

olivia: Implementation note: change read loop to select on ctx.Done() prior to blocking reads, so we can bail early. Example: for { select { case <-g.ctx.Done(): close(events); return default: } tok, err := dec.ReadToken() ... } That prevents blocking indefinitely if the stream remains open at transport layer.

neeraj: I built a quick patch combining B+C: replace detached retry goroutine with errgroup tied to the incoming ctx and add Close(). Local sampleapp e2e repro no longer shows lingering goroutines. Patch branch: gen-handshake-cancel-fix-2026.

tarun: Good. Please also add a small smoke test in sampleapp that cancels mid-handshake and asserts the main goroutine exits within a second. Relying on exact goroutine counts is flaky but os.Exit after short timeout is a decent assertion in integration tests.

olivia: CI note: add a comment in the auth shim clarifying why we removed the inner child ctx. We had that code to isolate refresh cancellations historically but it caused surprising behavior when the request owner expected cancel to close everything. A short comment avoids future regressions.

neeraj: I'll include sample code in the PR description showing proper client usage: create ctx, call client.Generator(ctx,...), consume Events() in goroutine, and either cancel ctx or call gen.Close() before exit. Also updated sampleapp README with a short troubleshooting note "app hangs on exit -> probably generator not closed / ctx not cancelled".

tarun: After CI green, we should run the flaky onboarding smoke e2e that previously surfaced this. If it passes, include the change in the next patch release and mention "generator / ctx cancellation improved" in the changelog.

ci-bot: Build started for gen-handshake-cancel-fix-2026 (build #4472).

olivia: One more thought: audit other SDKs for parity (JS/py) in behavior around mid-handshake cancellation so docs are consistent. If we add Close() here, confirm equivalent exists in other SDKs or add a migration note.

neeraj: Good call. I'll open a short cross-sdk issue and tag maintainers. Thanks team, this should make the Go onboarding a lot less brittle.
